summary:
Overall Goal:

To establish a defined area for a safe landing, identify an optimal area for conducting research, and determine multiple safe routes connecting the landing area to the research area on Mars using the Dijkstra Algorithm and various extraterrestrial topographical and meteorological maps.

Process of Work:

With the assistance of Artificial Intelligence (AI), we investigated and collected information to create multiple maps illustrating temperature distribution, temperature variations, surface elevation, wind direction and intensity, and various other environmental factors. Using this information, we aimed to identify a specific area that would provide the highest possible probability of a safe landing. We then identified the most suitable area for conducting research near the landing site, located close to Olympus Mons. Finally, using the Dijkstra Algorithm, we developed multiple safe and efficient routes connecting the previously identified landing area to the research area. We also created multiple maps illustrating the aforementioned environmental factors to further support, visualize, and solidify our idea.
details:
Steel Mars Run - Project Details Report

Report date: November 15, 2026
Scope: Source code, configuration, and data files in the project workspace

1. Project Overview and Goal

Steel Mars Run is a analysis application that uses extraterrestrial topography and atmospheric data to examine terrain conditions in a selected study area and generate exploratory landing-site and research-route candidates. Its interface is built with Streamlit. The default terrain study area is a triangle near Lycus Sulci, where the application analyzes slope and roughness. Landing candidates can be connected to a defined research zone on Mars using risk-weighted routes calculated with the Dijkastra Algorithm.

The overall goal is to make an early-stage screening and educational planning for Mars exploration more systematic. Viewing terrain shape, thermal conditions, wind, and dust in a shared map context can help users compare candidate areas and consider safe route options to a target region.

2. Process Of Work

2.1. Data input

The application supports two data-input paths selected from the sidebar: direct downloads from the PDS archive and local file uploads. Terrain data can be provided as a MOLA ENVI raster (.img with a matching .hdr and optional .lbl) or as a single-band, georeferenced GeoTIFF (.tif/.tiff). Atmospheric inputs include EMARS NetCDF (.nc) and Mars Climate Database (MCD) text output (.txt). PDS product discovery and download features are included. PDS URLs and public GitHub Release assets are subject to HTTPS, host and redirect validation, and file-size limits, so occasional errors may happen.

2.2 Processing workflow

2.2.1. Read the DEM and assess its data
ENVI headers provide raster dimensions, data type, byte order, NoData, scale/offset, and map/projection information. ENVI rasters can be opened using memory mapping. GeoTIFFs are read Github, specifically Rasterio; the application expects a single band, a geographic CRS, and an elevation unit that can be converted to pixels of which are measured in meters.
2.2.2. Analyze terrain
Slope is calculated using central differences, with horizontal distances derived from the Mars radius and pixel dimensions. Roughness is the RMS elevation residual from a least-squares plane fitted to each 3×3 window. The app displays elevation, regional slope, roughness maps, and summary statistics.
2.2.3. Prepare atmospheric layers
For EMARS files, users can select a time and pressure level. The program recognizes surface and atmospheric temperature, east-west and north-south wind components, and dust optical depth. MCD text blocks are parsed into latitude-longitude grids, with variable descriptions and units inferred where it is possible to do so. Atmospheric fields on different grids are interpolated onto the terrain grid before suitability analysis.
2.2.4. Calculate combined screening scores
Soft costs are calculated for slope, roughness, temperature, wind, and dust based on ideal ranges. The default weights are 25% for slope, 20% for roughness, 20% for temperature, 20%, and 15% for atmospheric conditions (wind and dust). A missing layer receives a neutral cost but lowers coverage and reliability. Valid sample counts also affect reliability. Up to 10 spatially separated landing candidates are ranked using 3×3 neighborhood support.
2.2.5. Plan routes to the research zone
Candidates are connected to traversable cells along the approach ring of a defined target polygon. The Dijkastra Algorithm searches an eight-neighbor grid and combines physical cell distance with the average risk of adjacent cells. Routes are ranked by total risk-weighted cost, and the interface reports route length and average layer values along each route.

3. Benefits

3.1. It reduces the need to switch manually between file formats and tools due to the programs ability to bring terrain and atmospheric data into a singular interface.
3.2. It does not automatically interpret missing data as safe. Reliability scores and layer coverage show what information supports a result.
3.3. Gradual thresholds help compare terrain near transition ranges without forcing every value into a strict suitable/unsuitable category.
3.4. The Dijkastra Algorithm routes let users consider access cost to the research area alongside the choice of a starting location.
3.5. The program supports multiple languages for users which require their language.

4. Limitations and Potential Flaws

4.1. Suitability thresholds and weights are illustrative starting assumptions and have not been calibrated against mission requirements.
4.2. A low-resolution DEM cannot identify small obstacles or hazards at vehicle scale such as a particularly small rock, slight changes of altitude, ect.
4.3. Atmospheric layers depend on selected time and pressure level, so comparisons require consistent conditions.
4.4. Interpolation and coverage calculations do not create higher-resolution information; the grid is the limit to the resolution of the information recieved.
4.5. No test suite or test data files were in the repository. This report is based on source-code and configuration review only. This means it does not imply mission validation or independent scientific validation.
4.6. Hardware inventory and team membership are not documented in the repository at all.

Potential next steps include adding high-resolution landing-hazard layers, tracking data-source and parameter versions, providing automated tests and sample datasets, analyzing sensitivity to weights and thresholds, comparing atmospheric time slices, and exporting results.

5. Tools and Technology

5.1. Programming language and libraries

5.1.1. Python - application logic and data processing.
5.1.2. Streamlit - interactive web interface and session state.
5.1.3. NumPy - raster and atmospheric arrays, statistics, and numerical calculations.
5.1.4. Rasterio / GDAL - GeoTIFF reading, raster metadata, and window operations.
5.1.5. xarray + netCDF4 - opening and selecting dimensions in EMARS NetCDF data.
5.1.6. SciPy - regular-grid interpolation, neighborhood operations, and related numerical tools.
5.1.7. Matplotlib - maps, layer plots, and route visualizations.
5.1.8. Requests - HTTP(S) downloads from PDS and GitHub Release sources.

(Dependency version ranges are specified in requirements.txt: Streamlit 1.40 to below 2.0; NumPy 1.26 to below 3.0; Matplotlib 3.8 to below 4.0; Requests 2.31 to below 3.0; Rasterio 1.4 to below 2.0; SciPy 1.12 to below 2.0; xarray 2024.10 or later; and netCDF4 1.7 or later.)

5.2. Data Formats and Development/Runtime Software

5.2.1. MOLA ENVI rasters and PDS label metadata.
5.2.2. EMARS atmospheric data in NetCDF format.
5.2.3. MCD text output in TXT format.
5.2.4. Single-band geographic GeoTIFF DEMs.
5.2.5. The documented local setup uses Windows PowerShell and a Python virtual environment.

5.3. Project Files / Structure

app.py, src/data_loader.py, src/geotiff_processing.py, src/terrain_analysis.py, src/analysis.py, src/terrain_plot.py, src/emars_processing.py, src/mcd_processing.py, src/site_suitability.py, src/route_planning.py, src/study_area.py, src/pds_download.py, src/i18n.py, data/processed/mars_study_area.tif

6. Original and Creative Aspects

The creative aspect is the integration of extraterrestrial topography and atmospheric layers into a singular workflow. Instead of displaying maps, the program connects data loading, area masking, terrain and atmospheric assessment, uncertainty and coverage reporting, landing-candidate ranking, and route planning to a target. It accounts for atmospheric data arriving on different grids and interpolates those fields onto the local DEM grid. Additionally, it also ranks routes using both distance between grid cells and a risk cost, rather than straight-line distance alone.

The thresholds in the code are explicitly provisional and documented as such. This makes the design adaptable: thresholds and weights can be recalibrated when mission requirements or higher-resolution data become available.
